title: Tennis Elbow/Tendinitis Rehab Program.
author: Matt B.
desc:
Smarter training means offloading the gripping muscles of the forearm while intentionally rebuilding the tendon's capacity.
​The primary culprit in tennis elbow is excessive strain from repetitive gripping and wrist extension. To heal, we will modify upper body movements to use neutral or palms-up grips, leverage lifting straps to eliminate grip strain, and prioritize floor-based or machine work.

Perform this 5-minute routine at the end of every single workout to actively heal the tendon tissue:

Eccentric Wrist Extensions: 3 sets of 15 reps. Rest your forearm on a flat bench with your palm facing down and your hand hanging off the edge. Use your healthy hand to lift a light dumbbell up into extension. Remove the healthy hand and take 4 full seconds to slowly lower the weight using only the injured arm.  

​Hammer Pronation/Supination: 3 sets of 15 reps. Hold a hammer or a light dumbbell by the bottom of the handle with your elbow at a 90-degree angle. Slowly rotate your forearm from palm-up to palm-down and back.  

​Forearm Extensor Stretch: 3 sets of 30 seconds. Hold your arm straight out, palm down, and gently pull your fingers down toward your body until you feel a gentle stretch across the top of the forearm.

A mild, dull ache (around a 2 or 3 out of 10 on a pain scale) during your rehab exercises is acceptable and normal as the tendon remodels. However, if any exercise causes sharp, stabbing pain, or if your elbow hurts significantly worse the next morning, you have overloaded the tendon. Immediately lower the weights or adjust your grip angles on the next session.

ex.note: Barbell Back Squat or Leg Press. 4 sets × 6–8 reps (Keep hands loosely resting on the bar; do not grip tightly).
3 sets × 10 reps per side (Hold dumbbells if your grip allows, or use a weighted vest/bodyweight to save the elbow).
3 sets × 12 reps.
3 sets × 12 reps.
Abs. 3 sets × 15 reps per side (Keep arms pointing straight up at the ceiling, no tension).
3 sets × 30-second holds (Squeeze your core and glutes; rest on your forearms to avoid hand pressure).
(With Lifting Straps): 4 sets × 10 reps. Use an underhand (supinated) grip or a close-grip neutral handle.
4 sets × 8 reps. (Floor presses limit the range of motion slightly, reducing stabilizing strain on the elbow joint).
(With Lifting Straps): 3 sets × 12 reps. Use a neutral grip attachment.
​Neutral-Grip Push-ups: 3 sets × Max Reps. Use dumbbells as handles so your wrists remain perfectly straight.
3 sets × 15 reps (Attach a wrist cuff to the cable instead of holding the rope to bypass the grip completely).

30–45 minutes of zone 2 cardio. An upright stationary bike or a steep incline treadmill walk is preferred. Avoid the rowing machine or elliptical, as both require continuous, repetitive hand gripping.
4 sets × 20–30 second holds.
3 sets × 20 reps per side (Perform bodyweight only or hold a light medicine ball gently against your chest).
3 sets × 12 reps per side (Focus on slow, deliberate extensions).
4 sets × 20 total steps (Bodyweight or weighted vest).
3 sets × 12 reps (Hug the dumbbell close to your chest with your forearms under the weight plates rather than gripping the handle).
​Glute Ham Raises or Nordic Curls: 3 sets × 8 reps.
Calf Raises (Seated/Leg Press or Standing Machine): 4 sets × 15 reps.
Forearm Side Planks: 3 sets × 30 seconds per side.
Inclinde Dumbell or Machine Press: 4 sets × 10 reps (Keep your wrists locked and completely straight under the load).
Chest-Supported Dumbbell or Machine Rows (With Lifting Straps): 3 sets × 12 reps. Keep your palms facing each other (neutral grip).
3 sets × 12 reps. If there is even minor discomfort, swap for open-palm cable bicep curls using a straight bar where the bar just rests on your open fingers.
3 sets × 15 reps (Focus on pushing down with the pinky side of your hand without strangling the rope).
Light Cardio Finisher: 15 minutes on the stairmaster or steady incline walk.
